props.title: The Driver
props.initialSlug: Pro getaway driver faces off against obsessed cop

sections.content: The Driver (1978) revolutionized car chase cinema with Walter Hill's minimalist approach and Ryan O'Neal's nameless getaway expert. It directly influenced later neo-noir films like Drive (2011) and Baby Driver (2017) with its stripped-down storytelling and emphasis on pure vehicular action. Hill's decision to keep characters unnamed (The Driver, The Detective, The Player) established a noir template that Nicolas Winding Refn would later perfect. The film's Los Angeles nightscape becomes a character itself, with neon-lit streets and empty parking garages creating a haunting urban playground for high-stakes pursuits.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond just chase sequences. Its economical dialogue and focus on professional criminals doing their jobs without melodrama created a new crime film language. Thief (1981) adopted a similar approach with James Caan's safe-cracker, while Le Samouraï (1967) had already established the template of the methodical criminal professional. The Driver's technical precision in shooting car sequences - emphasizing real stunts and mechanical authenticity - established benchmarks that influenced everything from The French Connection (1971) to Ronin (1998).

Hill's direction strips away standard action movie excess, focusing instead on the pure craft of driving and pursuit. This approach influenced a generation of filmmakers, from Michael Mann's methodical professionals in Heat (1995) to the wheel work in The Transporter (2002). The film's cat-and-mouse game between O'Neal and Bruce Dern's obsessed detective created a template for antagonist relationships that still resonates in modern thrillers. SUBHEAD: Evolution of the Professional Driver Genre

sections.content: The professional driver archetype established in The Driver evolved through various interpretations. To Live and Die in L.A. (1985) brought a grittier, more morally ambiguous take on pursuit driving, while Gone in 60 Seconds (2000) emphasized the pure joy of automotive excellence. The character type reached its artistic peak with Drive, which merged European art house sensibilities with American genre conventions, much as Hill's original film blended French New Wave influences with Hollywood action.
